newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Government plays down Stet defeat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Government plays down Stet defeat.

text.p: Italy's government on Thursday played down a parliamentary defeat over the transfer of telecom holding Stet to the Treasury but the incident showed that political opposition to privatisation still runs deep.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi was quoted as saying the defeat would not scupper Italy's ambitious privatisation programme and that the Treasury would still take charge of Stet as a first step towards preparing it for sale.
"With regard to the privatisation, nothing changes," Prodi told Italian media on his way to an official visit to Croatia.
The government narrowly lost a vote in the lower house of parliament on the transfer of Stet from state industrial holding IRI on Wednesday night by 230 to 234 with 26 abstentions.

The Treasury wants full control of Stet because it fears foot-dragging by IRI managers will hold up its privatisation. The move also allows the government to fulfil a commitment to slash IRI's huge debt.
Many members of the coalition, including several ministers, failed to turn up to vote, contributing to the defeat.

The Marxist-inspired Communist Refoundation party, whose votes are crucial to Prodi's government, abstained and the centre-right Freedom Alliance, led by former premier Silvio Berlusconi, mustered enough support to vote down the decree.

Cabinet undersecretary Enrico Micheli said the effect of the defeat was minimal because the 1997 budget, approved at the end of last year, had authorised the Treasury to acquire Stet from IRI and the transfer had already taken place.

The cabinet, which meets on Friday, is expected to propose a bill that would exempt IRI from capital gains tax on the sale. The Treasury said last month it would pay 14.53 trillion lire ($9.4 billion) to IRI for its controlling interest in Stet.

The Stet sale will stave off bankruptcy for the heavily indebted IRI, which has been ordered by the European Commission to cut its exposure to below five trillion lire by the end of June from 22.5 trillion at the end of 1995.

Financial markets appeared ready to give the government the benefit of the doubt. Stet's share price sank at the opening on Thursday to 7,210 lire from a closing price of 7,521 lire but by mid-session had recovered to 7,425 lire.

"Everyone knows this is the mother of all Italian privatisations and a lot of people are opposed to it," said an analyst at the Milan office of a leading European investment bank. "In practical terms it's a non-event because the transfer has already happened."
Stet's Managing Director Ernesto Pascale was less sanguine.
"For us it doesn't matter if IRI or the Treasury owns us. What does matter is to see that there are still doubts over the privatisations," Pascale told La Repubblica newspaper.
"One has the feeling that this country still hasn't understood the importance of the sell-offs," Pascale said.

Some analysts were surprised that the opposition, which has said it favours reducing the state's role in the economy, had voted against the decree. "It seems that no party in this country genuinely believes in the free market," said Giovanna Mossetti, an economist at Milan brokerage house Caboto.
It was not immediately clear whether the parliamentary defeat was a result of bad coordination or a boycott by some of the government's own supporters.

"If the latter is the case it's a real problem," said Mario Deaglio, a business commentator based in Turin. "Time will be wasted at a time when the state of the financial markets offers an excellent opportunity to privatise."

Economists say the government has a unique opportunity to sell off state assets to the public because many Italians have been on the lookout for alternatives to low-yielding treasury bills as interest rates come down.
